title: Normality can be tested over a perfect purely inseparable overfield
statement: Let $k\subseteq K$ be fields [def-weil-field, def-pc-field-extension]. Set $q=1$ in characteristic zero and $q=p$ in characteristic $p>0$. Assume that every $a\in K$ has $a^{q^n}\in k$ for some $n\ge0$, and that $K$ is perfect (the Frobenius $a\mapsto a^p$ is surjective when $p>0$). For any $k$-scheme $T$ [def-pc-scheme], the following are equivalent: (1) every local ring of $T_K=T\times_k\operatorname{Spec}K$ is an integrally closed domain [def-pc-fibre-product, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]; (2) for every field extension $L/k$, every local ring of $T_L$ is an integrally closed domain. No finite type, reducedness, nonemptiness or separatedness hypothesis is imposed on $T$.

source.place: Tag 038O, label lemma-geometrically-normal, equivalence (2) and (6); algebra.tex Tag 046W, label lemma-perfection, uniqueness identifies any perfect purely inseparable overfield with the perfect closure

proof.text: Assume (2). Its universal quantifier includes the given field extension $K/k$, so it gives (1) immediately.

For the converse assume (1), and fix an arbitrary extension $L/k$. Apply [lem-weil-common-extension-fields] to $K/k$ and $L/k$ to obtain embeddings into a common field $M$ agreeing on $k$. For each finitely generated subextension $E/K$ of $M/K$, [lem-weil-pbc-perfect-field-separating-basis] supplies a separating transcendence basis because $K$ has exactly its perfectness hypothesis. Thus every such $E/K$ is separably generated, and $M/K$ is separable in the nonalgebraic sense of [def-weil-pbc-separable-field-extension]. We do not assume $M/K$ is algebraic or finitely generated.

source.place: Tag 030Z (lemma-perfect), definition-perfect and Definition 030O (definition-separable-field-extension); common field: fields.tex Tag 0H7K (lemma-common-extension-field).

proof.text: Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be an affine open of $T$. For any extension $H/k$, its base change is $U_H=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_k H)$, and these are open subschemes covering $T_H$. Here the affine identification is checked by the universal properties: a ring map from $A\otimes_k H$ is precisely a pair of maps from $A$ and $H$ agreeing on $k$, hence a pair of spectrum maps; check on affine test schemes and glue. Base changing the inclusion gives the inverse-image open: maps into $T_H$ whose projection lands in $U$ are exactly the maps into $U_H$, by the same fibre-product property. Restricting a structure sheaf to an open does not change its stalk at a point in that open, since its neighborhoods contained in the open are cofinal. By (1), all stalks of $U_K$ are normal domains. The spectrum-stalk identification of [lem-weil-pbc-spec-domain-stalks-function-field](1) then says every prime localization of $A\otimes_k K$ is a normal domain, so this algebra is a normal ring by [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring].

source.place: Tag 038O (lemma-geometrically-normal), affine reduction (5); schemes.tex Tag 01HV (lemma-spec-sheaves), part (6).

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-normal-algebra-separable-scalar-extension] with base field $K$, normal algebra $B=A\otimes_k K$ from step 3, and separable extension $M/K$ from step 2. It proves that $(A\otimes_k K)\otimes_K M$ is normal. The ring isomorphism $(a\otimes c)\otimes m\mapsto a\otimes cm$, with inverse $a\otimes m\mapsto(a\otimes1)\otimes m$, identifies this algebra with $A\otimes_k M$. For $u\in K$, the outer balancing relation has equal images $a\otimes(uc)m=a\otimes c(um)$; $k$-balancing is $av\otimes cm=a\otimes vcm$ for $v\in k$. The inverse respects $k$-balancing because $(av\otimes1)\otimes m=(a\otimes v)\otimes m=(a\otimes1)\otimes vm$. Both maps preserve products and units. On generators their composites are the identity: $a\otimes m\mapsto a\otimes m$, and $(a\otimes c)\otimes m\mapsto(a\otimes1)\otimes cm=(a\otimes c)\otimes m$. A ring isomorphism identifies primes, localizations and monic equations in fraction fields, preserving normality. Thus $A\otimes_k M$ is normal.

source.place: Tag 0C3M (lemma-base-change-normal-by-separable), affine form, varieties.tex; tensor balancing identifies the iterated base change.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-normal-ring-field-extension-descent] with the field extension $M/L$ and $B=A\otimes_k L$. Define $\phi: (A\otimes_k L)\otimes_L M\to A\otimes_k M$ by $(a\otimes l)\otimes m\mapsto a\otimes lm$ and $\psi$ in the reverse direction by $a\otimes m\mapsto(a\otimes1)\otimes m$. For $c\in k$ the $k$-balancing identity is $ac\otimes lm=a\otimes clm$; for $u\in L$ the outer balancing identity is $a\otimes(ul)m=a\otimes l(um)$. Thus $\phi$ is well defined. For $\psi$, $ (ac\otimes1)\otimes m=(a\otimes c)\otimes m=(a\otimes1)\otimes cm$, so it is $k$-balanced. Both maps preserve products on pure tensors and send the unit to the unit. Their composites satisfy $\phi\psi(a\otimes m)=a\otimes m$ and $\psi\phi((a\otimes l)\otimes m)=(a\otimes1)\otimes lm=(a\otimes l)\otimes m$ by $L$-balancing, so they are inverse ring isomorphisms. Step 4 supplies normality of $A\otimes_k M$, hence of this scalar extension: a ring isomorphism identifies primes and their localizations, and maps monic polynomial equations and fractions bijectively, preserving the normal-domain condition. The descent lemma requires no algebraicity, separability or finite generation of $M/L$. Hence $A\otimes_k L$ is normal.

For each affine open $U$ chosen in step 3, step 5 and [lem-weil-pbc-spec-domain-stalks-function-field](1) show that every stalk of $U_L$ is an integrally closed domain. The opens $U_L$ cover $T_L$, and their stalks agree with those of $T_L$ by the cofinal-neighborhood argument in step 3. Consequently every local ring of $T_L$ is an integrally closed domain. Since $L/k$ was arbitrary, (2) follows. If $T$ is empty there are no stalks and both assertions are vacuous; no quasi-compactness or separatedness entered the affine argument.
